To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) pigs fed dried porine solubles or fermented soybean meal have improved ADG and G/F; (2) enzyme addition did not improve performance when DDGS is fed at 20% of the diet; (3) sorghum DDGs reduced G:F; and (4) pigs fed Peptone 1 and Peptone 3 had improved G:F.

(a) adding enzymes to diets containing DDGS did not improve pig performance (b) pigs fed dried porcin solubles had superior performance compared to pigs fed other specialty proteins and (c) pigs fed increasing inogranic P had improved bone ash and G:F.

(1) dried porcine soluble addition to a corn-soybean meal diet improved nursery pig growth and feed efficiency; (2) fermented soybean meal can partially replace fish meal in nursery pig diets; and (3) the addition of commercial phytases to nursery pig diets can improve bone mineralization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of specialty proteins, DDGS, or phytase to improve the economics of swine production.
improving the performance and health of pigs.
the effects of specialty proteins, enzymes, and DDGS on nursery pig performance and the effects of different phytases on available P release.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the addition of specialty proteins or enzymes in nursery diets may not improve pig performance.
adding dried porcine plasma to a corn and soybean meal diet, or adding enzymes to a DDGS diet, did not improve pig performance.
there is no evidence that adding specialty proteins to nursery pig diets improves growth performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the addition of dried porcine blood meal, fermented soybeans, and spray dried animal plasma to nursery pig diets improved pig performance.
the use of specialty proteins in nursery diets is beneficial to performance, and that the inclusion of phytase in nursery diets should be evaluated based on its ability to increase available P.
